reg-edict-of-milan.why: Diocletian’s Great Persecution, begun in 303, had failed to break the Church, and the dying emperor Galerius had already granted toleration in 311. Constantine, who credited the Christian God with his victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312, sealed an alliance with Licinius by marrying his half-sister to him.
reg-edict-of-milan.impact: Churches could now own property and build openly, and Constantine paid for great basilicas and gave clergy legal privileges. Bishops became public figures with access to the court, and in 325 the emperor himself summoned the Council of Nicaea to settle disputes over doctrine.

reg-battle-of-lechfeld.why: The Magyars had settled the Carpathian basin in the late ninth century and lived partly on plunder and tribute. In 955 they besieged Augsburg, hoping to exploit a recent rebellion against Otto led by his own son. Otto gathered troops from several German duchies, along with Bohemian allies, to relieve the city.
reg-battle-of-lechfeld.impact: Otto’s authority over the German dukes was strengthened, and the eastern frontier was reorganised into marches, one of which later grew into Austria. In Hungary the ruling Árpád family turned to diplomacy and conversion, and around the year 1000 Stephen I was crowned as a Christian king.

reg-battle-of-clontarf.why: Brian Boru came from the Dál Cais, a minor Munster dynasty, and had risen to break the long hold of the Uí Néill on the high kingship, winning recognition in 1002. About a decade later Leinster and the Norse town of Dublin revolted against his overlordship and sought allies overseas.
reg-battle-of-clontarf.impact: Later writers recast the battle as the Irish driving out the Vikings, although Irishmen fought on both sides and the Norse stayed on in Dublin as traders under Irish overlords. Brian’s descendants took the surname O’Brien and remained a leading family in Munster for centuries.

reg-pisa-tower-begun.why: Pisa was a wealthy maritime republic, enriched by Mediterranean trade and naval victories. Its citizens poured that wealth into a showpiece religious complex, beginning the cathedral in the 1060s and the baptistery in the 1150s. A free-standing bell tower was the third great building planned for the site.
reg-pisa-tower-begun.impact: The long pauses let the soil settle, which probably saved the tower from collapse, and later builders made the upper floors slightly taller on one side to compensate. It was closed in 1990 for stabilisation work that reduced the lean, and it reopened to visitors in 2001.

reg-ninety-five-theses.why: The preacher Johann Tetzel was selling indulgences near Wittenberg, with part of the proceeds helping Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz repay debts he had run up to gain his office. Luther had come to believe salvation came through faith alone, and the printing press gave his objections a ready audience.
reg-ninety-five-theses.impact: Luther was excommunicated in 1521 and refused to recant before the emperor at Worms. His German Bible shaped the written language, Western Christianity split into rival churches, and Europe saw more than a century of religious wars. The Catholic Church answered with its own reforms at the Council of Trent.

reg-gunpowder-plot.why: English Catholics faced fines and exclusion for refusing to attend Protestant services. Many hoped James I, the son of the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, would ease the laws, and were disappointed when he did not. Peace with Spain in 1604 also ended any realistic hope of foreign help.
reg-gunpowder-plot.impact: The surviving plotters were executed, and new laws required Catholics to swear an oath of allegiance and barred them from many professions. Suspicion of Catholics shaped English politics for generations, and full civil rights came only in 1829. The cellars of Parliament are still ceremonially searched before each State Opening.

reg-defenestration-of-prague.why: In 1609 Emperor Rudolf II had granted Bohemia’s Protestants freedom of worship in the Letter of Majesty. Tension rose when the staunchly Catholic Ferdinand of Styria was accepted as king in 1617, and disputes over Protestant churches built on Church land convinced the nobles that their rights were being withdrawn.
reg-defenestration-of-prague.impact: The rebels chose a Protestant king, Frederick of the Palatinate, but were crushed at White Mountain in 1620. Bohemia was forcibly returned to Catholicism and its crown made hereditary in the Habsburg line. The wider war lasted until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 and devastated the German lands.

reg-lisbon-earthquake.why: The earthquake came from a fault beneath the Atlantic south-west of Portugal, near the boundary of the African and Eurasian plates, though the exact source is still debated. It struck on the morning of All Saints’ Day, when much of the population of a crowded, wealthy city was at Mass.
reg-lisbon-earthquake.impact: Pombal sent a questionnaire to parishes across Portugal asking how the ground had moved, a survey often seen as an early step towards seismology. His handling of the crisis made him the dominant figure in government, and philosophers including Kant wrote about earthquakes as natural rather than divine events.

reg-london-underground-opens.why: London’s population had grown enormously, and the main railway stations had been kept at the edge of the centre, leaving streets choked with horse-drawn traffic. The City solicitor Charles Pearson campaigned for years for a railway to link the termini, and the Metropolitan Railway was built from Paddington to Farringdon.
reg-london-underground-opens.impact: The line was soon extended, and later branches opened up new commuter suburbs north-west of the city. Smoke in the tunnels remained a problem until electric trains arrived, first on a deep-level tube line in 1890. Budapest and Paris opened their own underground railways around the turn of the century.

reg-german-empire-proclaimed.why: Prussia had defeated Denmark in 1864 and Austria in 1866, bringing northern Germany under its leadership. War with France in 1870 persuaded the southern states, including Bavaria, to join. The date chosen, 18 January, was the anniversary of the first Prussian king’s coronation in 1701.
reg-german-empire-proclaimed.impact: France lost Alsace and much of Lorraine and paid a large indemnity, leaving lasting resentment. A populous, fast-industrialising power now sat at the centre of Europe, upsetting the old balance. Bismarck spent the next two decades building alliances to keep France isolated, a system that later hardened into rival blocs.

reg-franz-ferdinand-assassinated.why: Austria-Hungary had annexed Bosnia in 1908, angering Serbia and South Slav nationalists. The young conspirators were armed by members of the Black Hand, a secret society with links to Serbian military intelligence. The visit fell on 28 June, St Vitus’s Day, a date of deep significance in Serbian national memory.
reg-franz-ferdinand-assassinated.impact: Germany backed Vienna, Russia backed Serbia, and by early August most of the great powers were at war. Four empires had collapsed by the time it ended, and a South Slav kingdom, later called Yugoslavia, was created in 1918. Princip, too young to be executed, died in prison that same year.

reg-carnation-revolution.why: Portugal had been a dictatorship since the 1930s, first under Salazar and from 1968 under Marcelo Caetano. Since 1961 wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau had consumed much of the budget and sent many young men abroad as conscripts or emigrants. A book by General Spínola argued the wars could not be won.
reg-carnation-revolution.impact: Free elections were held a year to the day after the coup, and a new constitution followed in 1976. Hundreds of thousands of settlers returned from Africa as the colonies became independent in 1974 and 1975. Portugal joined the European Community in 1986, and 25 April is a national holiday.

reg-channel-tunnel-opens.why: Digging had started in the 1880s but was stopped amid British fears of invasion, and a 1970s scheme was cancelled over cost. In 1986 Margaret Thatcher and François Mitterrand signed a treaty for a privately financed rail tunnel, and boring machines from each side met under the sea in 1990.
reg-channel-tunnel-opens.impact: Eurostar trains linked London with Paris and Brussels, and shuttle trains began carrying cars and lorries. Passenger journeys to Paris fell to a little over two hours once Britain’s high-speed line was finished in 2007. Construction ran far over budget, leaving the operating company with heavy debts for years.

reg-prc-proclaimed.why: China had been divided since the fall of the Qing in 1911. Nationalists and Communists fought from 1927, pausing uneasily to resist Japan’s invasion. After 1945 the Nationalist government was weakened by corruption and runaway inflation, while the Communists had won wide support among peasants through land reform.
reg-prc-proclaimed.impact: The new state redistributed land, allied with the Soviet Union and fought in Korea within a year. Two rival governments now claimed to represent China, and Beijing took the country’s United Nations seat only in 1971. Mao’s later campaigns, the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, cost millions of lives.

reg-hiroshima-bomb.why: The United States had built the bomb in the Manhattan Project, begun out of fear that Germany would get there first, and tested it in New Mexico in July 1945. Japan fought on after Germany’s defeat. Historians still debate how American leaders weighed avoiding an invasion against other motives.
reg-hiroshima-bomb.impact: The Soviet Union’s declaration of war on Japan the same week added to the pressure to surrender. The bombings opened a nuclear arms race between the superpowers. Survivors, known as hibakusha, faced lasting illness and stigma, and Hiroshima became a centre of campaigning against nuclear weapons.

reg-meerut-uprising.why: Deeper grievances lay behind the cartridge scare. The Company had annexed Indian states, including Awadh in 1856, the home of many of its soldiers, and sepoys feared for their pay, status and religion. At Meerut, 85 troopers were publicly shackled and jailed for refusing the cartridges, and their comrades rose.
reg-meerut-uprising.impact: The rebels marched to Delhi and proclaimed the elderly Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, as their leader. He was later exiled to Rangoon, ending the dynasty. Britain reorganised the Indian army and promised not to interfere with religion. Later Indian nationalists remembered the revolt as a first war of independence.

reg-fall-of-saigon.why: The Paris Peace Accords of 1973 had withdrawn American combat troops but left the war unresolved. The United States Congress then cut aid to South Vietnam. When the North attacked in early 1975, a retreat from the Central Highlands turned into a rout, and the southern army collapsed within weeks.
reg-fall-of-saigon.impact: Many former southern officials and soldiers were sent to re-education camps, and hundreds of thousands of people fled the country by boat over the following years. The United States kept a trade embargo on Vietnam until 1994, and the defeat made American leaders wary of foreign military commitments.

reg-khomeini-returns.why: The Shah’s power had been restored by a coup in 1953, and he used oil wealth to drive rapid Westernising reforms while his secret police silenced critics. Khomeini was exiled in 1964 for denouncing him, and from Iraq and then France his sermons circulated in Iran on cassette tapes.
reg-khomeini-returns.impact: A new constitution gave ultimate authority to a senior cleric, with Khomeini as the first Supreme Leader. Iran’s alliance with the United States ended with the seizure of the American embassy in November 1979, where hostages were held for 444 days. Iraq invaded in 1980, beginning an eight-year war.

reg-qin-unification.why: Qin, on the western edge of the Chinese world, had been transformed in the fourth century BCE by the reforms of Shang Yang, which rewarded military merit, taxed farmers directly and centralised power. With a large disciplined army, its king conquered the six rival states one by one in about a decade.
reg-qin-unification.impact: The ruler took the new title huangdi, emperor, which Chinese monarchs used until 1912. Hereditary lords were replaced by appointed officials governing commanderies and counties, a structure the following Han dynasty kept. The name China itself is often thought to derive from Qin.

reg-sekigahara.why: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had unified Japan, died in 1598 leaving a five-year-old heir under a council of regents. Tokugawa Ieyasu was the richest and most powerful of them. Ishida Mitsunari, a loyal Toyotomi administrator, gathered a coalition of mainly western lords to stop him taking control.
reg-sekigahara.impact: Ieyasu confiscated and redistributed his enemies’ lands, became shogun in 1603 and governed from Edo, the future Tokyo. He destroyed the Toyotomi family at Osaka in 1615. Lords who had opposed him were kept out of high office, and two such domains, Satsuma and Choshu, led the shogunate’s overthrow in 1868.

reg-plassey.why: The young Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, resented the Company fortifying Calcutta without permission and abusing its trading privileges, and seized the town in 1756. Clive retook it. With Britain and France at war, and powerful Bengali bankers and courtiers plotting against the Nawab, the Company chose to replace him.
reg-plassey.impact: Mir Jafar became Nawab and paid enormous sums to the Company and its officers. In 1765 the Mughal emperor granted the Company the right to collect Bengal’s taxes, turning a trading firm into a territorial ruler. A catastrophic famine struck Bengal in 1770 under its administration.

reg-mongol-sack-baghdad.why: The Great Khan Möngke sent his brother Hülegü west in the 1250s to destroy the Nizari Ismaili strongholds in Persia and to bring the caliph to submission. Caliph al-Musta’sim refused the Mongol demands but did little to prepare the city’s defences, and Baghdad was surrounded by a far larger army.
reg-mongol-sack-baghdad.impact: Estimates of the dead vary enormously. Hülegü founded the Ilkhanate, which ruled Persia and Iraq for generations. The Mongol advance was halted in 1260 by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut, and Cairo, where a line of Abbasid caliphs was kept as figureheads, became the leading centre of Arab learning.

reg-wuchang-uprising.why: The Qing had been weakened by military defeats, foreign indemnities and reforms that came too late. Revolutionary groups had spread through the modernised New Army, and a plan to nationalise railways using foreign loans provoked protests in 1911. An accidental bomb blast exposed plotters near Wuchang, forcing them to act early.
reg-wuchang-uprising.impact: Sun Yat-sen became provisional president on 1 January 1912 but soon gave way to the general Yuan Shikai. After Yuan’s death in 1916 the republic broke up among rival warlords. The anniversary, 10 October, is still marked as the national day in Taiwan, known as Double Ten.

reg-hangul-promulgated.why: Korean had been written with Chinese characters, which fitted the language’s sounds and grammar poorly and took years of study that only the elite could afford. Sejong wanted commoners to be able to read laws and put their grievances in writing. Several consonant shapes reflect the position of the mouth and tongue.
reg-hangul-promulgated.impact: Many scholars at court opposed the new script and continued to write in Chinese, so for centuries it was used mainly by women and in popular fiction and letters. It gained official status only in the 1890s. Today it is the everyday script of both North and South Korea.

reg-cyrus-takes-babylon.why: Cyrus had already overthrown his Median overlords and conquered Lydia in western Anatolia, making Persia the strongest power in the region. Babylon’s last king, Nabonidus, had alienated the priests of Marduk by favouring the moon god Sin and by spending years away from the capital in Arabia.
reg-cyrus-takes-babylon.impact: Persia gained Mesopotamia, Syria and the Levant, creating the largest empire the world had yet seen. The Cyrus Cylinder presents him as a restorer chosen by Marduk. The Temple in Jerusalem was rebuilt under Persian rule, and Babylon stayed a great city but was never again an independent capital.

reg-battle-of-talas.why: Tang China had extended its power far into Central Asia along the Silk Road, while the Abbasids, who had just overthrown the Umayyad caliphs, were pushing east. A quarrel between two local kingdoms drew in both powers, and the Tang general Gao Xianzhi marched to meet the Abbasid army.
reg-battle-of-talas.impact: Neither side pressed further. A few years later the An Lushan rebellion pulled Tang troops home, ending Chinese power in the region for centuries, and Central Asia gradually became Muslim. Paper mills did appear in Samarkand, although paper may already have been reaching the region by trade.

reg-capture-of-malacca.why: Having reached India by sea in 1498, the Portuguese set out to control the spice trade at its sources and cut out Muslim and Venetian middlemen. Afonso de Albuquerque had taken Goa in 1510, and an earlier Portuguese trading mission to Malacca had ended with some of its men held captive.
reg-capture-of-malacca.impact: The sultan’s family went on to found the sultanate of Johor, and many Muslim merchants moved to rival ports such as Aceh, so Portugal never gained a true monopoly. From Malacca, Portuguese ships reached the Spice Islands and the coast of China within a few years.

reg-carthage-destroyed.why: After losing two wars, Carthage was forbidden to fight without Rome’s consent, yet it recovered its prosperity. When it finally took up arms against repeated encroachments by Rome’s ally Masinissa of Numidia, Rome had its pretext. The senator Cato the Elder had long pressed for the city’s destruction.
reg-carthage-destroyed.impact: In the same year Rome sacked Corinth, leaving it master of the Mediterranean. North Africa became a major source of grain for the city of Rome. Carthage was refounded as a Roman colony about a century later and grew into one of the largest cities of the western empire.

reg-cairo-founded.why: The Fatimids, an Ismaili Shia dynasty, had ruled from what is now Tunisia since 909 and claimed leadership of the whole Muslim world against the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad. Egypt was rich but had been weakened by famine and political disorder, and earlier Fatimid attempts to take it had failed.
reg-cairo-founded.impact: The caliph moved his court to the new city in 973, making it the capital of a rival caliphate. Al-Azhar became a lasting centre of learning and turned to Sunni teaching after Saladin ended Fatimid rule in 1171. Cairo gradually absorbed the older town of Fustat nearby.

reg-tondibi.why: Al-Mansur had gained prestige and ransom money from Morocco’s defeat of Portugal in 1578, and he wanted direct control of the gold trade and the Saharan salt mines at Taghaza. Songhai, meanwhile, had been weakened by succession disputes and civil war among its ruling family.
reg-tondibi.impact: Morocco found the conquest costly to hold across the desert, and the gold proved less than hoped. Its control faded within decades, and the region broke into smaller states. Scholars of Timbuktu, including Ahmad Baba, were deported to Marrakesh, and trade increasingly shifted towards the Atlantic coast.

reg-cape-town-founded.why: Dutch East India Company ships took months to reach Batavia, and crews died of scurvy for lack of fresh food. The Cape lay roughly halfway. Survivors of the Haarlem, wrecked in Table Bay in 1647, lived there for about a year and reported that the land was suitable for a supply station.
reg-cape-town-founded.impact: From 1657 the Company released men to farm on their own account, taking grazing land used by the Khoikhoi and leading to conflict. Enslaved people were brought from Asia, Madagascar and East Africa. The Afrikaans language developed there, and Britain took the colony permanently in 1806.

reg-liberia-independence.why: The Society was backed both by opponents of slavery and by slaveholders who wanted free Black people removed from the United States. The first settlers arrived in the 1820s. By the 1840s the Society was short of money, and British traders refused to pay customs duties to a colony that was not a sovereign state.
reg-liberia-independence.impact: Joseph Jenkins Roberts became the first president. Britain recognised the republic quickly, the United States only in 1862. The settlers’ descendants, a small minority, dominated politics and excluded the indigenous majority until a coup in 1980. Liberia was one of very few African states never colonised by a European power.

reg-victoria-falls.why: Livingstone, a Scottish missionary, believed that opening the African interior to commerce and Christianity would undermine the slave trade. He was following the Zambezi downstream during a crossing of the continent, looking for a navigable route to the coast, with men and canoes supplied by the Makololo chief Sekeletu.
reg-victoria-falls.impact: His account of the journey became a bestseller and made him a national hero in Britain, encouraging further missionary and commercial interest in central Africa. A railway bridge was built across the gorge in 1905. The falls are now a World Heritage Site and a major centre for tourism.

reg-isandlwana.why: Britain’s high commissioner, Sir Bartle Frere, wanted to join southern Africa into a single confederation and saw the independent Zulu kingdom as an obstacle. In December 1878 he sent Cetshwayo an ultimatum that included disbanding the Zulu army, terms the king could not accept, and British troops invaded without clear approval from London.
reg-isandlwana.impact: The defence of nearby Rorke’s Drift that night was celebrated in Britain to offset the shock. Reinforcements arrived, and the Zulu capital Ulundi was burned in July. Cetshwayo was exiled and his kingdom divided among thirteen chiefs, which led to civil war. Zululand was annexed in 1887.

reg-fall-of-khartoum.why: Egypt had ruled Sudan since the 1820s, and its heavy taxes were resented. In 1881 Muhammad Ahmad declared himself the Mahdi, a divinely guided leader, and his followers destroyed an Egyptian army in 1883. Britain, which had occupied Egypt the year before, decided Sudan should be abandoned.
reg-fall-of-khartoum.impact: Gladstone’s government was widely blamed for delaying the rescue. The Mahdi died of illness months after his victory and was succeeded by the Khalifa Abdallahi. An Anglo-Egyptian army under Kitchener reconquered Sudan in 1898, and the country was then run jointly by Britain and Egypt until independence in 1956.

reg-anglo-zanzibar-war.why: Zanzibar had become a British protectorate in 1890, and Britain insisted that no sultan could take the throne without its consent. British officials preferred Hamoud bin Mohammed, whom they expected to be more cooperative, particularly over ending slavery. Khalid barricaded himself in the palace with his guards and supporters.
reg-anglo-zanzibar-war.impact: About five hundred of the palace’s defenders were killed or wounded, against one British sailor injured. Khalid escaped to the German consulate and then to German East Africa. Hamoud was installed, and the legal status of slavery was abolished the following year. British control lasted until 1963.

reg-lucy-discovered.why: The Hadar site in Ethiopia’s Afar region lies in the Rift Valley, where erosion exposes ancient sediments and layers of volcanic ash allow them to be dated. The geologist Maurice Taieb had identified its promise, and the previous season Johanson had found a knee joint suggesting an upright walker.
reg-lucy-discovered.impact: With about forty per cent of a skeleton preserved, Lucy showed that human ancestors walked upright long before their brains grew large. Her species was named Australopithecus afarensis in 1978. In Ethiopia she is called Dinkinesh, meaning "you are marvellous", and her bones are kept in Addis Ababa.

reg-ebola-first-outbreak.why: The virus is thought to pass to people from wild animals, with fruit bats suspected as its natural host, though this is not proven. The outbreak centred on Yambuku in northern Zaire, where the hospital had very few syringes, and traditional funerals involving contact with the body spread it further.
reg-ebola-first-outbreak.impact: The outbreak killed about nine in ten of those known to be infected before quarantine and closing the hospital ended it. Isolation, protective clothing and safe burials became the standard response. An epidemic in West Africa from 2014 killed more than 11,000 people, and vaccines were approved in 2019.

reg-rwandan-genocide.why: Belgian colonial rule had hardened the division between Hutu and Tutsi with identity cards. A Hutu-led revolution from 1959 drove many Tutsi into exile, and their descendants’ rebel army invaded in 1990. Extremists resisted a 1993 peace deal, and the killing began after the president’s plane was shot down.
reg-rwandan-genocide.impact: Around two million people, mostly Hutu, fled to neighbouring countries, and the camps in Zaire helped spark wars there that killed vast numbers. A United Nations tribunal in Tanzania delivered the first genocide conviction by an international court in 1998, and Rwanda used community courts to try many others.

reg-world-cup-south-africa.why: South Africa had been barred from world football during apartheid and narrowly lost the vote to host in 2006. FIFA then decided the next tournament should go to Africa, and in 2004 South Africa was chosen ahead of Morocco and Egypt, with Nelson Mandela lending his support to the bid.
reg-world-cup-south-africa.impact: The country built or rebuilt stadiums and upgraded airports and rail links, though critics questioned the cost and several grounds were little used afterwards. The tournament passed without the security problems some had predicted. Ghana reached the quarter-finals, and Mandela’s appearance at the final was his last at a major public event.

reg-ben-ali-flees.why: Zine El Abidine Ben Ali had ruled since 1987. Unemployment was high, especially among young graduates in the neglected interior, and the wealth of the president’s family was widely resented. Protests spread through social media, satellite television and the trade unions, and the army did not move to crush them.
reg-ben-ali-flees.impact: Ben Ali went into exile in Saudi Arabia, where he died in 2019. Tunisia held free elections in 2011 and adopted a new constitution in 2014, and four civil society groups won the Nobel Peace Prize for brokering compromise. From 2021 President Kais Saied concentrated power in his own hands.

reg-pakal-palenque.why: Pakal came to the throne aged twelve at a low point for his city. Palenque had been attacked and sacked by the rival kingdom of Calakmul in the preceding years, and the ruling line had been disrupted. His mother, Lady Sak K’uk’, appears to have held power before him.
reg-pakal-palenque.impact: Under Pakal and his sons Palenque was rebuilt as a major power, with a palace and temples carrying unusually long inscriptions. Those texts helped scholars work out the city’s dynasty in the 1970s, a milestone in deciphering Maya writing. His jade mask and carved sarcophagus lid are world famous.

reg-jamestown.why: England wanted a share of the American wealth that Spain enjoyed, and an earlier colony at Roanoke had vanished. James I granted a charter in 1606 to investors who hoped for gold and a passage to Asia. The site was picked because it could be defended against Spanish ships.
reg-jamestown.impact: It became the first permanent English settlement in the Americas. In 1619 Virginia held the first representative assembly in English America, and the first recorded enslaved Africans arrived the same year. Tobacco plantations spread across Powhatan lands, leading to wars that broke the power of the local peoples.

reg-quebec-founded.why: French fishermen and traders had visited the St Lawrence since Jacques Cartier’s voyages in the 1530s, and beaver pelts were in demand for European hats. Earlier attempts at settlement had struggled. Champlain chose a spot beneath a high cliff, near the former Iroquoian village of Stadacona.
reg-quebec-founded.impact: Champlain allied with the Innu, Algonquin and Wendat against the Haudenosaunee, drawing France into conflicts that lasted most of a century. The colony grew slowly, but its French language, Catholic faith and legal traditions survived the British conquest. The old town is now a World Heritage Site.

reg-port-royal-quake.why: England captured Jamaica from Spain in 1655, and its governors encouraged buccaneers to base themselves there to defend the island and raid Spanish shipping. The town grew fast on a sand spit at the harbour mouth, with heavy brick buildings crowded onto loose, waterlogged ground.
reg-port-royal-quake.impact: Many more people died of disease and injuries in the weeks afterwards, and preachers presented the disaster as divine judgement. Fire and hurricanes ended attempts to rebuild, though the Royal Navy kept a base there. Kingston later became Jamaica’s capital, and the sunken town is an important underwater archaeological site.

reg-plains-of-abraham.why: During the Seven Years’ War the British government under William Pitt committed large forces to conquering New France. The fall of Louisbourg in 1758 opened the St Lawrence to the navy. Wolfe had besieged Quebec for nearly three months without success and needed a result before winter ice forced the fleet away.
reg-plains-of-abraham.impact: Montreal surrendered the following year, and France gave up Canada by treaty in 1763. Britain later guaranteed French civil law and Catholic worship in Quebec. With the French threat gone, the American colonies depended less on British protection, and taxes raised to pay for the war fed their discontent.

reg-louisiana-purchase.why: Spain had quietly returned Louisiana to France in 1800, alarming Jefferson, since western farmers relied on shipping goods through New Orleans. Napoleon had planned a new American empire, but his army in Saint-Domingue was destroyed by disease and Haitian resistance, and with war against Britain looming he needed money.
reg-louisiana-purchase.impact: The purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States, and all or part of fifteen states were later formed from it. Jefferson doubted whether the Constitution allowed it. The new land sharpened disputes over the spread of slavery and led to the displacement of many Native nations.

reg-alamo.why: Mexico had invited American settlers into Texas in the 1820s, and they soon outnumbered Mexicans there. Tension grew when Mexico restricted further immigration and moved against slavery, on which many settlers relied. In 1835 Santa Anna replaced the federal constitution with a centralised one, prompting revolts in Texas and other states.
reg-alamo.impact: Texas was an independent republic for nine years before joining the United States in 1845. That annexation helped bring on the Mexican-American War, in which Mexico lost about half its territory. The mission became a shrine of Texan identity, although historians continue to debate how its story is told.

reg-battle-of-puebla.why: Mexico was bankrupt after years of civil war, and in 1861 President Benito Juárez suspended payments on foreign debts. Britain, Spain and France sent forces to Veracruz. The first two withdrew once it was clear that France meant to conquer the country, while the United States was absorbed in its own civil war.
reg-battle-of-puebla.impact: The victory delayed the French by a year. They installed the Austrian archduke Maximilian as emperor in 1864, but withdrew under American pressure once the Civil War ended, and Maximilian was shot in 1867. The anniversary is now a bigger celebration among Mexican Americans than in most of Mexico.

reg-last-spike.why: British Columbia joined Canada in 1871 on the promise of a railway within ten years, but a bribery scandal brought down the government and delayed the work. Many feared the thinly settled West would otherwise be absorbed by the United States. Thousands of Chinese labourers built the hardest mountain sections.
reg-last-spike.impact: The line opened the prairies to large-scale farming settlement and created Vancouver as its Pacific terminus. In the same year Canada imposed a head tax on Chinese immigrants, now that their labour was no longer needed. For Indigenous peoples of the plains the railway brought rapid loss of land and independence.

reg-mexican-revolution.why: Díaz’s rule brought railways, foreign investment and order, but land became concentrated in great estates while villages lost their communal fields, and opposition was suppressed. He had hinted that he would retire, then stood again aged eighty. Madero, a wealthy reformer, escaped and called for an uprising on 20 November.
reg-mexican-revolution.impact: Díaz resigned within months, but Madero was overthrown and murdered in 1913. The constitution of 1917 promised land reform, labour rights and national ownership of mineral wealth, and limited the Church’s power. Estimates of the dead vary widely. A single party born of the revolution governed Mexico until 2000.

reg-halifax-explosion.why: Halifax was a principal port for assembling Atlantic convoys in the First World War, and its harbour was crowded. The Imo, a relief ship running late, was travelling on the wrong side of the channel. The Mont-Blanc flew no warning flag for its cargo, and crowds gathered to watch the fire.
reg-halifax-explosion.impact: Thousands were injured, many blinded by flying glass, which spurred better care for blind people in Canada. The city’s north end was flattened, and a blizzard the next day hampered the rescue. Boston sent a relief train, and Nova Scotia still sends that city a Christmas tree each year in thanks.

reg-cuban-missile-crisis.why: Fidel Castro’s revolution had aligned Cuba with the Soviet Union, and an American-backed invasion by exiles failed at the Bay of Pigs in 1961. Khrushchev wanted to protect Cuba and to offset the American lead in long-range missiles. A U-2 spy plane photographed the launch sites in October 1962.
reg-cuban-missile-crisis.impact: A direct hotline between Washington and Moscow was set up the next year, and the two powers signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere. The United States pledged not to invade Cuba. Khrushchev’s standing at home suffered, and he was removed from power in 1964.

reg-mexico-city-olympics.why: Mexico City was awarded the Games in 1963, making them the first held in Latin America. The government wanted to show off a modern, stable country after decades of economic growth. Through the summer of 1968 students protested against police repression and the cost of the event.
reg-mexico-city-olympics.impact: The thin air helped sprinters and jumpers and hindered distance runners, and Beamon’s record stood for almost 23 years. Dick Fosbury won the high jump with his backwards technique, soon copied by nearly everyone. Smith and Carlos were sent home, and their protest became a lasting image of the civil rights era.

reg-haiti-earthquake.why: Haiti lies on the boundary between the Caribbean and North American plates, and the magnitude 7.0 quake was shallow and close to the capital. Extreme poverty meant that most buildings were made of poorly reinforced concrete, built without enforced codes, in densely packed neighbourhoods on steep slopes.
reg-haiti-earthquake.impact: The death toll is disputed. The Haitian government put it above 300,000, while other estimates are much lower. More than a million people were left homeless. A cholera epidemic, introduced by United Nations peacekeepers later that year, killed thousands more, and reconstruction was slow despite large pledges of aid.

reg-cabral-brazil.why: After Vasco da Gama’s return from India in 1499, King Manuel sent Cabral with thirteen ships to establish trade there. Portuguese pilots swung west to catch favourable winds, and a treaty of 1494 had already assigned lands in that zone to Portugal. Whether the landfall was truly accidental is debated.
reg-cabral-brazil.impact: Portugal at first paid the new land little attention, valuing it mainly for brazilwood, a source of red dye that gave the country its name. Settlement began in earnest in the 1530s with sugar plantations worked by enslaved people. Brazil became the largest Portuguese-speaking nation in the world.

reg-lima-founded.why: Pizarro had captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 and entered Cusco the following year. The Spaniards first set up a capital at Jauja in the mountains, but it was too high and too far from the sea. The new city was named the City of the Kings.
reg-lima-founded.impact: Pizarro was assassinated in Lima in 1541 by a rival faction of conquistadors. A university was founded there in 1551, among the oldest in the Americas. For much of the colonial period, Spanish South America’s legal trade had to pass through its port of Callao. About a third of Peruvians live there today.

reg-potosi-silver.why: The Spanish were already mining at nearby Porco when, by tradition, an Indigenous man named Diego Huallpa came across the ore on the mountainside. The hill held one of the richest silver deposits ever found, but it stood more than 4,000 metres up in a cold, barren landscape.
reg-potosi-silver.impact: In the 1570s Viceroy Toledo organised a rotating labour draft and introduced mercury refining, greatly raising output. Spanish silver coins became a currency accepted around the world, and historians link the flow of bullion to rising prices in Europe. Mining on the mountain continues, and the town is a World Heritage Site.

reg-buenos-aires-garay.why: The Spanish settlement at Asunción, far up the Paraguay River, needed an outlet to the Atlantic. Juan de Garay had already founded Santa Fe on the way downstream. He set out from Asunción with settlers, most of them born in the colony, and with cattle and horses.
reg-buenos-aires-garay.impact: Spain required the region’s trade to go overland through Lima, so contraband with Portuguese and other foreign merchants flourished. In 1776 the city became capital of a new viceroyalty and was opened to legal trade. Its people repelled two British invasions and in 1810 set up their own government.

reg-tupac-amaru-ii.why: José Gabriel Condorcanqui was an educated local chief and mule trader who claimed descent from the last Inca ruler and took his name. Spanish reforms had raised sales taxes, and officials forced Indigenous communities to buy goods at inflated prices. His attempts to win redress through the courts had failed.
reg-tupac-amaru-ii.impact: The fighting and reprisals killed tens of thousands of people. A related revolt under Túpac Katari besieged La Paz in 1781. Spain abolished the forced sale of goods but also suppressed Inca titles, dress and symbols. Later movements across Latin America adopted the rebel leader’s name.

reg-portuguese-court-rio.why: Napoleon demanded that Portugal close its ports to Britain, its old ally. When Portugal hesitated, a French army invaded in late 1807. The Prince Regent João sailed with thousands of courtiers and the royal treasury under British naval escort, shortly before French troops entered Lisbon.
reg-portuguese-court-rio.impact: Rio gained a royal library, a botanical garden, a national bank and a printing press. Brazil was raised to a kingdom in 1815. When João returned to Lisbon in 1821 his son Pedro stayed and declared independence the next year, so Brazil remained united under a monarchy while Spanish America fragmented.

reg-venezuela-independence.why: Napoleon’s removal of the Spanish king in 1808 left the colonies without a legitimate ruler. In April 1810 leading citizens of Caracas deposed the Spanish governor and formed a junta. The Creole elite wanted free trade and self-government, and Francisco de Miranda and the young Bolívar pressed for a complete break.
reg-venezuela-independence.impact: Venezuela was among the first Spanish American colonies to declare full independence. A severe earthquake in 1812 struck republican-held towns, and royalist clergy called it divine punishment. Victory at Carabobo in 1821 finally secured the country, which formed part of Gran Colombia until 1830. The date, 5 July, is the national day.

reg-boyaca.why: After repeated defeats in Venezuela, Bolívar had rebuilt his army on the Orinoco plains with local horsemen and British and Irish volunteers. He decided to strike New Granada instead, leading his troops across flooded grasslands and over a high Andean pass in the rainy season, which the royalists had not expected.
reg-boyaca.impact: Bolívar entered Bogotá days later, gaining its treasury and a secure base. From there his armies went on to free Venezuela and Ecuador over the next three years. The union he created broke apart around 1830. The anniversary, 7 August, is a national holiday in Colombia.

reg-darwin-galapagos.why: The Beagle had sailed in 1831 under Robert FitzRoy to chart the coasts of South America for the Admiralty. Darwin, then 22, joined as a naturalist and companion to the captain on the recommendation of his Cambridge professor. The islands were a stop on the way home across the Pacific.
reg-darwin-galapagos.impact: Darwin did not grasp the significance of his specimens at once. Back in London the ornithologist John Gould showed that his finches were separate, closely related species, which set him thinking about how species change. The islands are now a national park, a World Heritage Site and a research centre.

reg-paraguayan-war.why: The states of the River Plate basin were rivals for territory and river access. When Brazil intervened in Uruguay’s civil war in 1864, Paraguay’s ruler Francisco Solano López saw a threat to the regional balance. He seized a Brazilian steamer, invaded Brazil, then attacked Argentina when it refused his army passage.
reg-paraguayan-war.impact: Paraguay lost territory to both Brazil and Argentina and was occupied for several years. Estimates of its population loss vary widely, but adult men were hardest hit. In Brazil the war made the army a political force and fed debate about slavery, both factors in the monarchy’s later fall.

reg-war-of-the-pacific.why: Deposits of guano and nitrate, used for fertiliser and explosives, had made the empty Atacama valuable. An 1874 treaty barred Bolivia from raising taxes on Chilean firms there. When it did so and moved to seize the company, Chile occupied the port of Antofagasta. Peru was drawn in by a secret alliance with Bolivia.
reg-war-of-the-pacific.impact: Chilean troops occupied Lima for more than two years. Peru ceded Tarapacá, and the status of Tacna and Arica was settled only in 1929. Nitrate taxes funded the Chilean state for decades. Bolivia took its claim to the International Court of Justice, which ruled in 2018 that Chile need not negotiate.

reg-lei-aurea.why: Abolition came in stages. The Atlantic slave trade to Brazil ended in 1850 under British pressure, and an 1871 law freed children born to enslaved mothers. In the 1880s a mass abolitionist movement grew, enslaved people fled plantations in large numbers, and the army refused to hunt them. Princess Isabel signed as regent.
reg-lei-aurea.impact: Several hundred thousand people were freed, but they received no land, schooling or other support, and the resulting inequality has lasted. Coffee planters turned increasingly to European immigrant labour, especially Italians. Landowners angered by the law withdrew their backing from the monarchy, leaving it with few defenders.

reg-valdivia-earthquake.why: Off Chile the Nazca plate slides beneath South America, and in 1960 about a thousand kilometres of that boundary ruptured. At magnitude 9.5 it is the strongest earthquake ever recorded. Powerful foreshocks the previous day had already driven many people out of their houses.
reg-valdivia-earthquake.impact: Deaths were relatively few for so large a quake, with estimates ranging from about one thousand to several thousand. Landslides dammed the outlet of Lake Riñihue, and workers dug channels for weeks to prevent a flood. The disaster spurred international cooperation on tsunami warnings across the Pacific.

reg-chile-coup.why: Allende, a Marxist, had been elected in 1970 with just over a third of the vote. He nationalised copper mines and banks and sped up land reform. By 1973 Chile faced soaring inflation, shortages, strikes and a deadlocked Congress, and the United States had worked covertly to weaken his government.
reg-chile-coup.impact: Allende died in the palace, by suicide according to later investigations. Congress was closed and parties banned. Official commissions later counted more than 3,000 people killed or disappeared and tens of thousands tortured. The regime imposed sweeping free-market reforms, and Pinochet lost a plebiscite on his rule in 1988.

reg-dirk-hartog-landing.why: A few years earlier Dutch captains had adopted a new route to Java, running east from the Cape of Good Hope on the strong westerly winds before turning north. It roughly halved the voyage, but sailors could not measure longitude, and ships that turned too late met the Australian coast.
reg-dirk-hartog-landing.impact: The coast appeared on Dutch charts under the name of Hartog’s ship, the Eendracht, and later voyages mapped much of what they called New Holland. The Dutch found the shore barren and without trade, so they did not settle. Several Company ships were later wrecked on the same coast.

reg-wallis-tahiti.why: After the Seven Years’ War, Britain and France competed to explore the Pacific. The Admiralty sent Samuel Wallis to search for a great southern continent that geographers believed must exist. His companion ship became separated near the Strait of Magellan, and his crew, weakened by scurvy, badly needed fresh food.
reg-wallis-tahiti.impact: The French explorer Bougainville arrived less than a year later, and his account of Tahiti as an earthly paradise shaped European ideas about the Pacific. The island became a regular port of call, bringing disease, firearms and, from 1797, missionaries. France made it a protectorate in 1842.

reg-bounty-mutiny.why: The voyage was promoted by Sir Joseph Banks to carry breadfruit to the West Indies as cheap food for enslaved plantation workers. The crew spent about five months in Tahiti, and many formed attachments there. Bligh’s sharp tongue and his quarrels with Fletcher Christian contributed, though the causes remain debated.
reg-bounty-mutiny.impact: A warship sent in pursuit seized the men who had stayed on Tahiti, and three were eventually hanged. The Pitcairn settlement was found in 1808, with one mutineer still alive. Their descendants live on Pitcairn and Norfolk Island. Bligh later completed a second breadfruit voyage and governed New South Wales.

reg-australian-gold-rush.why: Earlier gold finds in New South Wales had been kept quiet by officials who feared disorder in a convict colony. When the Californian rush of 1849 drew men away, the government offered a reward for a workable goldfield. Hargraves took the credit, although his local helpers did much of the actual panning.
reg-australian-gold-rush.impact: Australia’s population nearly tripled in ten years, and Melbourne became one of the richest cities in the British Empire. Miners’ anger over licence fees led to the Eureka Stockade revolt of 1854 and to wider voting rights. Hostility towards Chinese diggers produced the first laws restricting immigration by race.

reg-first-melbourne-cup.why: Gold had made Melbourne rich in a single decade, and its people had a passion for horse racing and betting. The Victoria Turf Club devised a two-mile handicap with a large prize to outshine a rival club. Flemington, beside the Maribyrnong River, had been used for racing since 1840.
reg-first-melbourne-cup.impact: The Victoria Racing Club took over the race a few years later. By the 1870s Cup Day was a public holiday in Melbourne, and crowds of around a hundred thousand were attending by the 1880s. Held on the first Tuesday in November, it is known as the race that stops a nation.

reg-fiji-cession.why: Cakobau, the chief of Bau, claimed to be king of all Fiji but could not control his rivals. He was pressed by American demands for compensation, and a cotton boom in the 1860s brought unruly European settlers and a brutal trade in Pacific labourers. His own government, set up in 1871, went bankrupt.
reg-fiji-cession.impact: The first governor, Sir Arthur Gordon, ruled through Fijian chiefs and blocked further sales of Fijian land, so most land stayed in Indigenous hands. A measles epidemic in 1875 killed a large share of the population, perhaps a quarter or more. Tension between the two main communities later lay behind several coups.

reg-tonga-constitution.why: King George Tupou I had united Tonga after years of civil war and had adopted Christianity. He had already issued law codes, including one in 1862 that freed commoners from forced service to chiefs. He wanted Tonga recognised as a state under international law, so that no foreign power could justify annexing it.
reg-tonga-constitution.impact: The constitution forbade selling land to foreigners, a key protection. Germany, Britain and the United States signed treaties recognising the kingdom. Britain handled its foreign affairs from 1900 to 1970 but never ruled it directly. The constitution is still in force, amended in 2010 so that most of parliament is elected by the people.

reg-ned-kelly-glenrowan.why: Kelly was the son of an Irish convict and grew up in a poor farming family in north-east Victoria that clashed repeatedly with police and wealthy landholders. After a disputed incident with a constable in 1878 he fled into the bush, and his gang killed three policemen and robbed two banks.
reg-ned-kelly-glenrowan.impact: A royal commission into the Victorian police followed, leading to dismissals and reforms. Kelly, who wore home-made armour beaten from plough parts, became a folk hero to some and a murderer to others. His story was filmed in 1906 in what is often called the first feature-length film.

reg-hawkes-bay-earthquake.why: New Zealand sits on the boundary of the Pacific and Australian plates. The magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck in mid-morning, when shops and offices were busy. Many buildings were of brick with heavy ornamental fronts, not designed for shaking, and broken water mains left firefighters unable to stop the blaze.
reg-hawkes-bay-earthquake.impact: With 256 deaths it remains New Zealand’s deadliest earthquake. It led to the country’s first national standards for earthquake-resistant building and, later, to a state disaster insurance scheme. Neighbouring Hastings was rebuilt largely in Spanish Mission style, and the region’s 1930s architecture now draws many visitors.

reg-sydney-harbour-bridge.why: A crossing had been proposed since the early nineteenth century, and by the 1920s ferries were carrying tens of millions of passengers a year. The engineer John Bradfield championed the project for decades. The contract went to the English firm Dorman Long, and construction took about eight years.
reg-sydney-harbour-bridge.impact: The bridge opened Sydney’s north shore to suburban growth, carrying trains, trams and road traffic. Building it gave work to many men during the Depression, and sixteen died on the job. The construction loan was paid off only in 1988. A harbour tunnel opened in 1992 to relieve congestion.

reg-castle-bravo.why: After the Soviet Union tested an atomic bomb in 1949, the United States pushed ahead with the far more powerful hydrogen bomb. Its first thermonuclear device, in 1952, was too bulky to use as a weapon. Bravo tested a solid-fuel design, at Bikini Atoll, whose people had been relocated in 1946.
reg-castle-bravo.impact: At about 15 megatons it was the largest American test ever. The death of a Lucky Dragon crewman months later stirred an anti-nuclear movement in Japan and helped inspire the film Godzilla. Worldwide alarm about fallout built pressure for the 1963 treaty banning atmospheric tests. Bikini remains uninhabited.

reg-samoa-independence.why: New Zealand’s rule was discredited early when its officials let the 1918 influenza epidemic ashore, killing about a fifth of the population. A non-violent independence movement, the Mau, grew in the 1920s, and police shot dead several marchers in 1929. After 1945 the United Nations oversaw steps towards self-government.
reg-samoa-independence.impact: Samoa was the first Pacific island nation to regain independence in the twentieth century. It signed a treaty of friendship with New Zealand, where a large Samoan community now lives. The constitution built in the traditional system of chiefly titles, and universal suffrage came only in 1991. New Zealand formally apologised in 2002.

reg-rainbow-warrior.why: France had tested nuclear weapons in French Polynesia since 1966, moving the tests underground in the 1970s after protests and legal action by New Zealand and Australia. Greenpeace planned to lead a flotilla to the test zone, and French officials authorised their secret service to stop the ship in Auckland harbour.
reg-rainbow-warrior.impact: A photographer, Fernando Pereira, drowned on board. France’s defence minister resigned and the head of the secret service was dismissed. Under a settlement mediated by the United Nations, France apologised and paid compensation. New Zealand wrote its nuclear-free policy into law in 1987, and France ended its Pacific tests in 1996.

reg-christchurch-earthquake.why: The magnitude 6.3 quake broke along a previously unknown fault very close to the city, producing exceptionally violent shaking. It struck at lunchtime on a weekday, when the centre was full. Many buildings were already weakened, and the city’s silty, waterlogged soils turned to liquid in many suburbs.
reg-christchurch-earthquake.impact: The earthquake killed 185 people, 115 of them in a single office building whose design a royal commission later found deficient. Thousands of homes on badly damaged land near the Avon River were bought by the government and cleared. New Zealand tightened its rules on strengthening earthquake-prone buildings nationwide.
